items.prompt: What is a 'transaction', as defined in L1?
choices: A group of operations treated as a single unit: they all succeed together, or the system undoes anything that already happened
Any single database write, no matter what
A log file that records every request a server receives
A retry mechanism that keeps attempting a failed operation
items.explanation: A transaction's defining property is treating multiple operations as one indivisible unit — not a synonym for any single write or a retry mechanism.
items.reference:
Transaction
📦 Multiple operations, one unit
✅❌ All succeed, or none do
Why: this is what turns "partially done" from a possible outcome into an impossible one.

items.prompt: According to L1, whose fault was the bug in the order/stock scenario — a bug in the stock decrement, a bug in the order insert, or something else?
choices: Neither individual step was wrong — nothing treated the two steps as one indivisible unit
The stock decrement had a bug that needed fixing
The order insert had a bug that needed fixing
Both steps had unrelated bugs that happened to occur together
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that neither step individually did anything wrong — the missing piece was treating both steps as one atomic unit.
items.reference:
Transaction
📦 Multiple operations, one unit
✅❌ All succeed, or none do
Why: this is what turns "partially done" from a possible outcome into an impossible one.

items.prompt: What do the four letters in 'ACID' stand for?
choices: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Availability, Concurrency, Integrity, Delivery
Atomicity, Caching, Indexing, Deduplication
Auditing, Consensus, Idempotency, Deployment
items.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — the four guarantees a real transaction system provides.
items.reference:
ACID
A: all-or-nothing
C: rules always hold
I: no seeing half-finished work
D: survives a crash
Why: each letter guards against a different way a multi-step write can go wrong.

items.prompt: According to L1, what does 'Durability' guarantee?
choices: Once a transaction reports success, that result survives a crash immediately afterward
The database will never lose power
A transaction can never take more than one second to complete
Every transaction is automatically backed up to a second data center
items.explanation: Durability is specifically about a reported success surviving an immediate subsequent crash — not about hardware uptime or backup infrastructure.
items.reference:
ACID
A: all-or-nothing
C: rules always hold
I: no seeing half-finished work
D: survives a crash
Why: each letter guards against a different way a multi-step write can go wrong.

items.prompt: What is a 'rollback', as defined in L1?
choices: Undoing every change made so far in a transaction, restoring the exact state from before it started
Reverting an entire application to a previous deployed version
Retrying a failed operation with a longer timeout
Deleting a database table entirely
items.explanation: A rollback specifically undoes a transaction's in-progress changes, restoring the pre-transaction state — not a deployment or infrastructure operation.
items.reference:
Rollback / commit
↩️ Rollback: undo everything so far
✅ Commit: make it permanent
Why: rollback is the default response to failure, not a bolted-on special case.

items.prompt: What is a 'commit', as defined in L1?
choices: Making a transaction's changes permanent and visible, only once every operation in it has succeeded
Saving a file to a version control system
Sending a confirmation email to a customer
Locking a database table so no one else can read it
items.explanation: A commit is specifically what happens after every operation in a transaction succeeds — it's what makes the changes permanent and visible.
items.reference:
Rollback / commit
↩️ Rollback: undo everything so far
✅ Commit: make it permanent
Why: rollback is the default response to failure, not a bolted-on special case.

items.prompt: What is a 'write-ahead log', as defined in L1?
choices: A durability mechanism: changes are written to a persistent, append-only log before the system reports success
A log of every error a server has ever encountered
A record of who accessed a system and when, for security auditing
A changelog documenting new features in each software release
items.explanation: A write-ahead log is specifically a durability mechanism — writing to persistent storage before acknowledging success, so a crash immediately after can still recover the change.
items.reference:
Write-ahead log
📝 Written before success is reported
🔁 Recoverable after a crash
Why: this is what makes durability possible even across a crash.

items.prompt: According to L1, when is a change written to the write-ahead log, relative to when success is reported?
choices: Before success is reported
After success is reported, as a background cleanup step
Only if the transaction is later rolled back
L1 doesn't specify the order
items.explanation: The log entry is written before the system reports success — that ordering is precisely what makes the log recoverable after a crash.
items.reference:
Write-ahead log
📝 Written before success is reported
🔁 Recoverable after a crash
Why: this is what makes durability possible even across a crash.

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, is rollback a special case bolted on afterward, or the transaction system's default response?
choices: The default response to any failure
A rare special case, only used for the most severe bugs
Something a developer must manually trigger every time
The flowchart doesn't include a rollback path at all
items.explanation: L2 states explicitly that rollback is the default response to failure, not a special case — which is why the naive version's bug can't happen inside a real transaction.
items.reference:
The transaction lifecycle
Begin → operate → check
Pass → commit; Fail → rollback
Why: nothing is visible until commit, which is what makes isolation possible.

items.prompt: According to L2, what makes isolation possible in the transaction lifecycle?
choices: Nothing is visible to the rest of the system until the commit step
Every transaction runs on a separate physical server
Transactions are limited to one operation each
Isolation isn't related to the commit/rollback lifecycle at all
items.explanation: L2 ties isolation directly to visibility only happening at commit time — nothing mid-transaction is exposed to other transactions.
items.reference:

Pass → commit; Fail → rollback

choices: 7 — the stock decrement happened even though the order was never created
10 — nothing changed since the order failed
0 — the entire stock was wiped out

items.explanation: L3 verifies stock drops to 7 (from 10, minus the 3-unit order) even though the order insert fails and orders.length stays 0 — the exact bug from L1.

The naive bug, verified
Stock: 10 → 7
Orders: still 0
Why: step 1 already happened by the time step 2 threw.

The transaction commits, leaving stock at -5

Order for 15, only 10 in stock

items.prompt: Implement `runTransaction(store, operation, invariant)`, matching L3: clone `store` into a `working` copy, run `operation(working)`, check `invariant(working)` if provided, and either commit (copy `working` back into `store`, return `{ committed: true }`) or leave `store` untouched and return `{ committed: false, error }` if anything throws or the invariant fails.

tests.description: commits a valid order, updating stock and orders
tests.expr: (() => { const store = { stock: { widget: 10 }, orders: [] }; const result = runTransaction(store, (w) => { w.stock.widget -= 3; w.orders.push({ orderId: 'o1' }); }, (s) => s.stock.widget >= 0); return expect(result.committed && store.stock.widget === 7 && store.orders.length === 1).toBeTruthy(); })()

tests.description: rolls back and leaves store untouched when the operation throws
tests.expr: (() => { const store = { stock: { widget: 10 }, orders: [] }; const result = runTransaction(store, (w) => { w.stock.widget -= 3; throw new Error('boom'); }, (s) => s.stock.widget >= 0); return expect(!result.committed && store.stock.widget === 10 && store.orders.length === 0).toBeTruthy(); })()

tests.description: rolls back when the invariant fails, even without a thrown error
tests.expr: (() => { const store = { stock: { widget: 10 }, orders: [] }; const result = runTransaction(store, (w) => { w.stock.widget -= 15; w.orders.push({ orderId: 'o2' }); }, (s) => s.stock.widget >= 0); return expect(!result.committed && store.stock.widget === 10 && store.orders.length === 0).toBeTruthy(); })()

items.explanation: This is the exact transaction wrapper L3 verifies against the naive version's bug — operating on a cloned `working` copy and only touching `store` at the very end (the commit step) is what makes rollback the natural, default outcome of any failure, rather than something that has to be remembered.
items.reference:
The transaction lifecycle
Begin → operate → check
Pass → commit; Fail → rollback
Why: nothing is visible until commit, which is what makes isolation possible.

items.prompt: Implement `durableCommit(log, entry)`, matching L3: append `entry` (serialized as JSON) to the `log` array, and return `{ acknowledged: true }`.

tests.description: appends the entry to the log as a JSON string
tests.expr: (() => { const log = []; durableCommit(log, { orderId: 'o1', productId: 'widget', qty: 3 }); return expect(log.length === 1 && JSON.parse(log[0]).orderId === 'o1').toBeTruthy(); })()
(() => { const log = []; const result = durableCommit(log, { orderId: 'o1', productId: 'widget', qty: 3 }); return expect(result).toEqual({ acknowledged: true }); })()

(() => { const log = []; durableCommit(log, { orderId: 'o1', productId: 'widget', qty: 3 }); durableCommit(log, { orderId: 'o2', productId: 'widget', qty: 2 }); return expect(log.length).toBe(2); })()

items.explanation: This models the moment a real database fsyncs a write to disk before acknowledging success — L3's point is that this write has to happen before the acknowledgement, which is exactly what makes the log recoverable after a crash.

items.prompt: Implement `recoverFromLog(log)`, matching L3: starting from a fresh store with `{ stock: { widget: 10 }, orders: [] }`, replay every entry in `log` (parsing each with `JSON.parse`), decrementing stock and pushing each order, and return the resulting state.

tests.description: matches L3's verified recovery: stock at 5, 2 orders, after a simulated crash
tests.expr: (() => { const log = [JSON.stringify({ orderId: 'o1', productId: 'widget', qty: 3 }), JSON.stringify({ orderId: 'o2', productId: 'widget', qty: 2 })]; const recovered = recoverFromLog(log); return expect(recovered.stock.widget === 5 && recovered.orders.length === 2).toBeTruthy(); })()

tests.description: returns the initial state unchanged for an empty log
tests.expr: (() => { const recovered = recoverFromLog([]); return expect(recovered.stock.widget === 10 && recovered.orders.length === 0).toBeTruthy(); })()

tests.description: preserves order details from the log entries
tests.expr: (() => { const log = [JSON.stringify({ orderId: 'o1', productId: 'widget', qty: 3 })]; const recovered = recoverFromLog(log); return expect(recovered.orders[0].orderId).toBe('o1'); })()

items.explanation: This is exactly how a real database recovers after a crash — replaying the durable log from scratch reconstructs the same state that existed right before the crash, which is what L3 verifies by discarding the in-memory store entirely and rebuilding from the log alone.
